key_terms.meaning: A written document that fixes what will be tested, how, by whom, when, and the rules for starting, stopping and resuming testing.
The conditions that must hold before a test phase may start, for example the build compiles and the smoke tests pass.
The conditions that must hold before testing is declared complete, for example all high-priority cases run and no critical defect is open.
The rules for pausing testing when the build is too broken to test, and the rules for restarting it after a fix.
A person whose main work is designing, running and reporting tests rather than writing product code.
How testers are organised: a central independent team, testers embedded in each product team, or a shared services pool.
The number of runs at which money saved by automation equals the cost of building and maintaining the scripts: n = build cost ÷ (manual cost per run − automated cost per run).
A number computed from test or defect data, such as pass rate or defect density, that supports a specific decision.
Defects found per unit of product size, such as defects per 1000 lines of code (KLOC) or per function point.
An immutable snapshot record in version control holding the changed files, a message, an author and the id of its parent commit.
A movable name pointing at one commit, so a line of work can go forward without disturbing other lines.
The act of joining two branches by combining their changes into one new commit on the target branch.
A commit or release that is formally frozen and used as the reference against which later changes are compared.
Merging every developer's work into the mainline at least once a day and proving each merge with an automatic build and test run.
Keeping the mainline in a state that can be released to production on demand, with every release step automated except the final approval.
The build, test and deploy steps kept as a versioned text file inside the repository instead of being clicked together in a tool's screen.
Ordering a pipeline so the cheapest, highest-signal checks run first, so a bad change is rejected within minutes rather than hours.
The versioned output of a build, such as a jar, war or container image, built once and then promoted unchanged to every environment.
The property that running the same automation any number of times leaves the system in the same state as running it once.
A YAML file listing ordered tasks that bring named hosts to a declared state, usually written to be idempotent.

takeaways: A test plan earns its name only when entry criteria, exit criteria and suspension rules are written as measurable statements, not as wishes.
Testing staffed as a small central team, as embedded testers, or as a shared pool each push risk ownership to a different place, so structure is a management decision, not an accident.
Automate a test only when it will be run many times and rarely changed; the decision is a break-even calculation, not an enthusiasm.
A metric is a decision aid; once it becomes a target, people optimise the number instead of the quality it was meant to stand for.
Version control gives exact rebuilds of any past state, which is what makes bisecting a defect, reverting a bad release and auditing a change possible.
Continuous integration is a habit plus a machine: merge to the mainline daily and let an automatic build and test run judge every merge.
A pipeline should build the artifact once and promote the same bytes through every environment, so what you tested is what you release.
Configuration management replaces hand-edited servers with a declared state that a playbook can recreate on any number of machines, every time.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on the parts of a plan, the people-and-structure side of testing, cost-based reasoning about automation, and how commits flow through a CI/CD pipeline to a tested artifact.

bank.q: A test plan is described as the written agreement for a test project. List the components a complete test plan must contain and explain why each one exists.
outline: Plan identifier, scope and objectives
Features to be tested and features not tested, with reasons
Approach, deliverables, environment, tools and test data
Entry criteria, exit criteria, suspension and resumption rules
Roles and responsibilities, schedule, risks and contingencies, approvals

bank.q: Distinguish entry criteria, exit criteria and suspension/resumption criteria, and give one measurable example of each for a web application release.
outline: Definition of each criterion and who agrees it
Entry: build compiles, smoke suite passes, test data loaded
Exit: all priority-1 cases run, pass rate ≥ 95%, zero open critical defects
Suspension: more than 20% of cases blocked; resumption: blocking defect fixed and verified
Why measurable criteria prevent endless or premature testing

bank.q: Explain the organisation structures used for testing teams and the skills expected of a test specialist, and describe how a technical training programme is built for such a team.
outline: Central independent test team, embedded testers, shared services pool: advantages and drawbacks of each
Independence versus product knowledge trade-off
Skills: test design, domain knowledge, tool and script writing, defect reporting, communication
Training plan: skill gap list, mentoring, pairing with developers, certification and lab practice
Career path and retention of test specialists

bank.q: Explain how a version control system stores project history as snapshots, and define commit, branch, merge, conflict and baseline.
outline: Repository stores objects identified by hash; a commit points to a tree of file blobs and to its parent
Commit as an immutable snapshot of the whole project at that moment
Branch as a movable pointer to a commit; cheap creation encourages parallel work
Merge and conflict: two changes to the same lines need a human decision
Baseline and audit trail: frozen reference for release and traceability

bank.q: A regression suite of 300 cases takes 5 person-hours per manual run and is run 40 times a year. Automation costs ₹4,80,000 to build and ₹40,000 a year to maintain, and a run then needs 0.5 person-hour of attention. Using a loaded rate of ₹800 per hour, compute the break-even number of runs and advise the team.
outline: Manual cost per run = 5 × 800 = ₹4,000
Automated cost per run = 0.5 × 800 = ₹400
Savings per run = ₹3,600; yearly maintenance ₹40,000
Break-even n = (build cost + maintenance) ÷ savings per run, about 145 runs, i.e. over three years at 40 runs a year
Recommendation: automate only the stable, high-frequency subset; state assumptions and sensitivity

bank.q: Design a build and test pipeline for a Java web application that must reach a testable artifact in under fifteen minutes. Name each stage, the check it performs and the order, and justify the order using fail-fast.
outline: Trigger on every push to the mainline and on pull requests
Stage 1: compile plus unit tests; Stage 2: static analysis and dependency scan
Stage 3: build the artifact once and store it with a version tag
Stage 4: deploy to a staging environment matching production, run integration, API and smoke tests
Stage 5: publish report, notify, promote artifact; fail-fast ordering keeps feedback under fifteen minutes

bank.q: Write an Ansible playbook that installs a web server on a group of staging hosts, copies a configuration file, restarts the service only when the file changes, and is safe to run repeatedly. Explain each part.
outline: Inventory file naming the hosts and host group
Play with hosts, become, tasks list
Package task ensuring the web server package is present
copy task with a handler notification; handler restarts the service
Explanation of idempotence, variable and template use, and what happens on the second run

bank.q: A release finds 40 defects in testing and 10 in the first month after release, with 200 defects reported by users over the product life so far. Compute defect removal efficiency and defect density for a product of 50 KLOC, and explain what each number is telling the manager.
outline: Formula for defect removal efficiency: defects found before release ÷ total defects, expressed as a percentage
Defect density = defects ÷ size in KLOC, with units stated
Interpretation: what a high or low value signals about the review and test process
Limits of both metrics: depend on size measure, defect counting rules and user reporting behaviour

bank.q: A manager sets 95% statement coverage as a target for every module and links part of the team bonus to it. Analyse what will happen to the test suite and to product quality over two releases.
outline: Coverage measures code executed, not behaviour verified
Testers write assertion-free tests that raise the number without finding defects
Target becomes a ceiling: work stops at 95%
Goodhart's law: a measure used as a target stops being a good measure
Better use: coverage as a diagnostic, paired with defect detection and escaped-defect data

bank.q: Explain how test planning, test team structure and test reporting fit together in a project that runs for nine months with three releases, and how you would report progress to a steering committee at each release.
outline: Plan sets scope, entry/exit criteria per release and resumption rules
Team structure decides who owns which risk and who signs off each release criterion
Reporting rhythm: daily build status, weekly defect trend, release readiness report
Report content: criteria met or not, defect open/close rates, coverage of planned cases, risks and contingency actions
Link between exit criteria and the go/no-go decision

bank.q: Compare long-lived feature branches with trunk-based development, and analyse the effect of each on integration risk, merge conflicts and the value of a continuous integration pipeline.
outline: Feature branch: isolation, but drift from mainline and large painful merges
Conflict probability grows with branch age and number of files touched
Trunk-based: small commits, frequent integration, short-lived branches behind feature flags
CI is meaningful only when merges are frequent; a pipeline on a rarely merged branch hides breakage
Recommendation with conditions: code review, flags, and discipline on incomplete work

bank.q: A team has budget to automate only part of its 600-case regression suite. Set out the criteria you would use to choose which tests to automate and which to keep manual, and justify turning some tests down.
outline: Criteria: frequency of execution, stability of the feature, data setup feasibility, risk level, cost of a missed defect
Keep manual: one-off, exploratory, usability and visual checks, hard-to-observe timing behaviour
Avoid automating tests that change every sprint; maintenance cost dominates
Portfolio view: smoke, API and data-driven tests first; fragile UI tests last
Decision recorded with expected runs per year and a review date

bank.q: A company releases once a month, with a two-week manual regression cycle and frequent rollbacks. Propose a plan to move to continuous delivery, covering test plan changes, metrics to track, pipeline stages and the risks you accept.
outline: Baseline measurement: release frequency, lead time, change failure rate, mean recovery time
Plan changes: exit criteria shift from full regression to risk-based automated smoke plus targeted regression
Pipeline: build once, artifact versioning, automated tests at each stage, same artifact promoted to staging and production
Release techniques: blue-green or canary, feature flags to separate deploy from release
Risks and mitigations: flaky tests, environment drift, missing test data, rollback drill; phased targets over releases

glossary.def: A unique name and version number given to a test plan so that reviewers and auditors can refer to an exact document.
A test plan section that records what is deliberately out of scope and why, so that no one assumes it was covered.
The test plan section listing what could disrupt testing and the prepared response for each, such as a backup environment or a second test data set.
A periodic record of which test cases ran, their results, and the defects raised, used to track progress during a phase.
The document issued at the end of a test phase that states results against exit criteria and gives a recommendation on release.
A table mapping each requirement to the test cases that cover it, used to show coverage and find untested requirements.
The inputs and preloaded records a test needs, prepared and versioned so that a run can be repeated exactly.
The configured hardware, software, network and data on which tests run, ideally close to production.
A small, fast set of checks that confirms the build is stable enough for deeper testing.
The set of tests rerun after every change to confirm that working behaviour has not been broken.
A test that passes and fails on the same code, usually due to timing, shared data or ordering, and which erodes trust in the whole suite.
Running two identical production environments and switching traffic from the old one to the new one, so rollback means switching back.
Sending a small share of live traffic to the new version first, watching error rates, then widening the share.
A configuration switch in the code that turns a feature on or off without redeploying, so deploy and release become separate acts.
Keeping staging and production close in operating system, versions, configuration and data shape, so tests predict real behaviour.
A build output that is never edited after creation; any change produces a new version with a new identifier.
Software such as Maven, Gradle or Make that compiles sources, resolves dependencies and packages the artifact from a declared recipe.
A branching style where developers commit to a single mainline in small, frequent changes, using short-lived branches at most.
A branch cut from the mainline to stabilise and patch one released version while new work continues on the trunk.
A merge situation where two branches changed the same lines of a file and a human must choose the final content.
The ordered, tamper-evident history of commits, messages, authors and dates that shows who changed what and when.
The command that sends local commits to a remote repository so other people can see and build them.
The practice of describing the required state of servers, packages, files and services in code and applying it repeatably.
A file listing the hosts and host groups that a playbook will act on, optionally with host-specific variables.
An Ansible task that runs only when notified by another task, typically used to restart a service after a configuration change.
